output:
The Huns, an enormous Tartar horde from beyond the Don and Volga, burst into the lands north of the Euxine around A.D. 372 and began working westward, almost exterminating the Alans before falling upon the Goths. The Ostrogoths made a desperate attempt to defend the Dniester against these "shapeless black collops of flesh," but were crushed and compelled to become vassals, save a remnant who fought southward to the Wallachian shore. The Visigoths under Duke Fritigern fell back in dismay with their wives, children, wagons, and flocks until they found themselves with their backs to the Danube, finding surrender to the enemy more dreadful than to their eastern brethren, as they were more civilized and mostly Christian. Pressed against the Roman border, the Visigoths sent in despair to ask permission to cross from the Emperor, with a contemporary writer describing how they stood stretching out their hands with loud lamentations, earnestly supplicating leave to cross and promising faithful adherence to the imperial alliance if the boon was granted (pp. 61-62).

At this moment (A.D. 376) the Roman Empire was again divided, with the house of Constantine gone and the East ruled by Valens, described as a stupid, cowardly, and avaricious prince who obtained the diadem only because he was the brother of Valentinian, the greatest general of the day. Valentinian had taken the West for his portion, dwelling in his camp on the Rhine and Upper Danube, while Valens, slothful and timid, shut himself up with a court of slaves and flatterers in Constantinople. The proposal of the Goths filled Valens with dismay, as it was difficult to say which was more dangerous: to refuse passage to 200,000 desperate men with arms in their hands and a savage foe at their backs, or to admit them within the line of river and fortress that protected the border. After much doubting, he chose the latter alternative, stipulating that if the Goths gave hostages and surrendered their arms, they should be ferried across the Danube and permitted to settle as subject-allies within the empire (pp. 62-63).

The Goths accepted the terms, gave up the sons of their chiefs as hostages, and streamed across the river as fast as the Roman Danube-flotilla could transport them. But no sooner had they reached Moesia than troubles broke out; the Roman officials at first tried to disarm the immigrants, but the Goths were unwilling to surrender their weapons and offered large bribes to be allowed to retain them. In strict disobedience to the Emperor's orders, the bribes were accepted and the Goths retained their arms. Further disputes soon broke out, as the provisions of Moesia did not suffice for so many hundred thousand mouths, and Valens had ordered stores of corn from Asia to be collected for the use of the Goths till they should have received and commenced to cultivate land of their own. However, the governor Lupicinus, to fill his own pockets, held back the food and doled out what he chose to give at exorbitant prices. In sheer hunger, the Goths were driven to barter a slave for a single loaf of bread and ten pounds of silver for a sheep, and the poorer immigrants were actually beginning to sell their own children for slaves rather than let them starve (pp. 63-64).

This drove the Goths to desperation, and a chance affray set the whole nation in a blaze. Fritigern, with many of his nobles, was dining with Count Lupicinus at Marcianopolis when some starving Goths tried to pillage the market by force. A party of Roman soldiers strove to drive them off and were at once mishandled or slain. On hearing the tumult and learning its cause, Lupicinus recklessly bade his retinue seize and slay Fritigern and the other guests at his banquet. The Goths drew their swords and cut their way out of the palace. Then riding to the nearest camp of his followers, Fritigern told his tale and bade them take up arms against Rome. There followed a year of desperate fighting all along the Danube and the northern slope of the Balkans. The Goths, half-starved for many months and smarting under the extortion and chicanery to which they had been subjected, soon showed that the old barbarian spirit was but thinly covered by the veneer of Christianity and civilization which they had acquired in the last half-century. The struggle resolved itself into a repetition of the great raids of the third century, with towns sacked and the open country harried in the old style, nor was the war rendered less fierce by the fact that many runaway slaves and other outcasts among the provincial population joined the invaders (pp. 64-65).
